title: Gap-entropy conjecture
formal: Are there absolute constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\) such that, for every Gaussian best-arm instance \(I\) defined below and every \(0<\delta<1/10\), \[cH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)\leq L(I,\delta)\leq CH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)?\] Here \(L\) is the order-oblivious instance-wise optimum over globally correct sampling algorithms, not the performance of one algorithm required to attain the bound on every instance.
why: The conjecture predicts the full instance-sensitive cost of identifying the best alternative, including the cost of learning which gap scales matter. Its entropy term would explain why instances with the same total inverse-square gap can have different exploration costs at fixed confidence.
status_note: A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 explicitly claims a positive resolution of this exact Gaussian instance-wise conjecture. Its Theorem 1.1 matches the target and its separate uniform-algorithm theorem addresses the related conjecture. This 13 September review has not independently checked the entire proof or located an established validation, so the status is uncertain, not source-open and not certified resolved.

category_assignment.reason: Best-arm identification is a pure-exploration bandit problem within the accepted optimization scope.

importance.reason: A central instance-sensitive sample-complexity conjecture in pure exploration, with a precise adaptation cost beyond the usual inverse-square gap sum; a fresh matching proof claim is explicitly flagged.

sentences: The arms have independent Gaussian rewards with unit variance and a unique best mean.
The benchmark averages expected sample cost over arm relabelings and takes an infimum over globally correct algorithms.
The conjecture predicts that cost from the total inverse-square gaps and the entropy of their scale distribution.
It differs from asking one algorithm to attain the benchmark on all instances without an adaptation cost.
A 9 September 2026 preprint claims the precise formula; its proof has not been independently certified in this review.

definitions: An instance has \(n\geq2\) independent arms with distributions \(\mathcal N(\mu_i,1)\), unknown means \(\mu_i\in[0,1]\), and a unique largest mean \(\mu_*\) at index \(*\). Each pull of arm \(i\) reveals a fresh independent sample from its distribution. An adaptive sampling algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\delta\), chooses pulls using earlier samples and independent internal randomness, and eventually outputs an arm index. It is \(\delta\)-correct if on every valid instance it stops almost surely and outputs its unique best arm with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Local computation is unrestricted; the resource is total number of pulls, and expectations include sampling noise and algorithmic randomness. Algorithms are measurable so that these probabilities and expectations are defined. Let \(T_A(I)\in[0,\infty]\) be the expected number of pulls. If \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of arm labels and \(\pi I\) is the corresponding relabeled instance, define \(L(I,\delta)=\inf_A (1/n!)\sum_{\pi\in S_n}T_A(\pi I)\), where the infimum ranges over algorithms correct on every instance of the same Gaussian model. The infimum is taken separately for each \(I,\delta\): an algorithm selected for favorable performance at I must nevertheless remain correct on all other instances. It need not attain the infimum. For each suboptimal arm, set \(\Delta_i=\mu_*-\mu_i\in(0,1]\), and \(H(I)=\sum_{i\ne *}\Delta_i^{-2}\). For integers \(r\geq0\), set \(G_r=\{i\ne *:2^{-(r+1)}<\Delta_i\leq2^{-r}\}\), \(H_r=\sum_{i\in G_r}\Delta_i^{-2}\), and \(p_r=H_r/H(I)\). The gap entropy is \(\operatorname{Ent}(I)=\sum_{r:p_r>0}p_r\log(1/p_r)\), with natural logarithms. Only finitely many groups are nonempty. The constants in the conjecture are independent of n, all means, the number of gap scales and δ.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of both uniform constant-factor bounds, or prove that no such universal pair of constants exists. A result only as δ tends to zero with the instance fixed, only for dyadic gaps or monotone algorithms, or an algorithm with an extra closest-gap term does not by itself prove the displayed claim about L. The recent claimed proof must meet the same mathematical and Lean-checking requirement.

context_blocks.text: This card selects Chen and Li’s Conjecture 3.5, which gives an explicit formula for the instance-wise optimum. Their separate Conjecture 3.2 asks for one algorithm attaining that optimum up to an additive two-arm adaptation term. The two statements are related but are not interchangeable.

Averaging over relabelings prevents an algorithm from gaining an artificial advantage because the best arm was placed at a preferred index. Taking an infimum over globally correct algorithms still permits a different favored sampling schedule for each target instance; it does not allow an algorithm to simply output a known best label without verifying correctness elsewhere.

Gap entropy weights a scale by its share of the inverse-square sampling burden, not by its fraction of arms. It vanishes when all gaps fall in one group and can grow when many scales carry comparable burden. The specified dyadic endpoint convention includes gaps equal to one; changing boundary conventions affects the full proposed complexity by at most constant factors.

Chen, Li and Qiao’s 2017 progress gives a nearly matching algorithmic bound and a lower bound for dyadic-gap instances under a monotonicity condition on algorithms. These restrictions and extra factors are relevant because the conjecture quantifies over all Gaussian instances and all correct algorithms.

A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 by Aronow, Kallus and Lopatto states the displayed two-sided result as Theorem 1.1. It also states a separate uniform-algorithm theorem with the closest-gap adaptation term. The present review matched their definitions and theorem statements, but has not independently certified the complete proof.

Asymptotic confidence-optimal algorithms study δ tending to zero for a fixed instance, when log(1/δ) eventually dominates its fixed entropy. Such a limit does not determine the uniform cost when gap scales and confidence vary together. This is why the nonasymptotic quantifiers matter.
